title: Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway
summary: The UCL Energy Institute's assessment of nuclear propulsion offers little immediate relief, confirming it is currently more expensive than conventional shipping. Economic viability hinges entirely on unproven reactor cost reductions and a robust IMO Net-Zero Framework, potentially making it competitive only after 2040. This stark reality underscores the industry's continued reliance on cheaper, high-carbon fuels, while "low-carbon pathways" remain distant and speculative.
content:
The report, Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway, was published by researchers from the UCL Energy Institute’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group, part of The Bartlett School of Environment, Energy and Resources.

The research found that without the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework (NZF), no nuclear-powered vessel is cheaper than a conventional ship, even at the lowest assumed reactor costs. With the NZF, nuclear propulsion could become the cheapest option from 2040, but only if reactor costs fall to levels not yet demonstrated.

Abstract

This study assesses the economic viability of nuclear-powered merchant shipping through a literature review, expert interviews and a total cost-of-ownership analysis.

The findings show that reactor costs and global greenhouse gas emissions policy are critical to the competitiveness of nuclear propulsion. Without the IMO Net-Zero Framework, no nuclear-powered vessel is cheaper than conventional ships currently in use, even at the lowest assumed reactor costs.

Under the NZF, nuclear propulsion could become the cheapest option from 2040, provided reactor costs fall significantly. However, these lower costs have not yet been demonstrated.

The research also identifies insurance, liability and regulatory frameworks as important barriers to adoption.

Published ahead of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) meeting, scheduled for 30 November –3 December 2026, the report highlights the importance of effective global emissions policy in determining whether nuclear propulsion can become a competitive low-carbon option for shipping.
